sections.body_md:
Four facts from linear algebra do almost all of the bookkeeping for linear state models, and none of them requires a particular physical plant. Rank counts independent directions. The null space is every vector a matrix sends to zero. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors describe directions the matrix only stretches. A similarity \(P^{-1}AP\) changes coordinates and leaves the eigenvalues alone, so the natural modes do not depend on which variables were called the states.

For a square matrix the rank-nullity theorem says rank plus the dimension of the null space equals the number of columns. A matrix with a zero eigenvalue is exactly a matrix with a nontrivial null space. That single link is why a controllability or observability matrix is tested by rank: a lost direction is a mode you cannot reach or cannot see.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\),
\[ \det A = ad - bc, \qquad \mathrm{tr}\, A = a + d. \]
Eigenvalues solve \(\det(\lambda I - A) = 0\), which for \(2 \times 2\) is
\[ \lambda^2 - (\mathrm{tr}\, A)\,\lambda + \det A = 0. \]
The sum of the eigenvalues is the trace. Their product is the determinant. A nonzero vector \(v\) is an eigenvector when \(Av = \lambda v\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\). The trace is \(9\) and the determinant is \(20 - 2 = 18\). The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2 - 9\lambda + 18 = (\lambda - 6)(\lambda - 3)\). The eigenvalues are \(6\) and \(3\). Check: \(A\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} = 6\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(A\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}\).

Separately, \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) has determinant \(0\), rank \(1\), and null vector \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\). And \(C\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}\) with \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) gives \(x = 1\), \(y = 2\): from \(5x + y = 7\) and \(2x + 3y = 8\), elimination produces \(13y = 26\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Writing \(\lambda^2 + (\mathrm{tr})\lambda + \det\). The trace term is subtracted in \(\det(\lambda I - A)\).
- Calling a matrix full rank because no entry is zero. A matrix can have every entry nonzero and still have rank \(1\).
- Confusing the column space (everything \(A\) can produce) with the null space (everything \(A\) kills).
- Expecting a change of coordinates to change the eigenvalues. It changes the eigenvectors' coordinates, not the eigenvalues.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Reachability stacks the columns \(B, AB, A^2B, \ldots\) and asks whether the rank equals the number of states. Observability stacks \(C, CA, CA^2, \ldots\) and asks the same question. Pole placement chooses a gain so the closed-loop matrix has a characteristic polynomial you picked. The coefficient of \(s\) in that monic polynomial is the sum of the desired poles.
